sourceLessons.title: Let Genesis use a browser
sourceLessons.prerequisites: A supported browser. Browser Bridge setup for your own browser.

steps.title: Choose the browser route
steps.narrationDraft: Genesis has its own browser workspace with tabs and persistent Genesis sign-ins. To use your already-open personal browser, connect Browser Bridge. These are different routes. A browser inside Genesis does not automatically share every login from your personal browser.
steps.checkpoint: You know which browser route you want.

steps.title: Connect your own browser in Computer use
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Computer use → Control. Find your browser and use Set up when offered. Follow the extension setup for that exact browser. Connection status belongs to the browser where the extension is installed; setting up Chrome does not also connect Edge.
steps.checkpoint: The intended browser reports connected or paired.

steps.title: Understand the connection status
steps.narrationDraft: A browser that was paired but is closed may reconnect when opened. A disconnected browser is not necessarily missing its extension. Check the name and state before repeating setup. Any app, Genesis browser, Your browsers (Browser Bridge) and Documents & spreadsheets control different kinds of access.
steps.checkpoint: You can identify the connected browser and its allowed control.

steps.title: Ask for a simple browser task
steps.narrationDraft: Try a public page first: “Open this page and tell me its three main points.” You can watch the integrated browser using View → Browser. A site may block automation or require sign-in; a working connection does not guarantee access to every website.
steps.checkpoint: The correct page opens and the summary matches it.

steps.title: Take control for a request that needs you
steps.narrationDraft: If a site asks for sign-in, a code or CAPTCHA, use the request or browser handoff. Take control prevents Genesis from using that control surface while you act. Finish the required step yourself, then use Resume to return browser control. That does not automatically resume a paused mission or finished model turn.
steps.checkpoint: You understand the handoff and can return control deliberately.

steps.title: Leave advanced browser tuning until needed
steps.narrationDraft: In Voice & Vision, browser settings choose profile, channel, headless mode, the inside-Genesis panel and page timing. Headless hides the browser. Page-settle time lets a page finish loading; navigation gaps slow repeated visits. Choose visible browsing while learning so you can follow the actions.
steps.checkpoint: Your first browser task runs in a view you can observe.

steps.title: Start with the main control categories
steps.narrationDraft: The Control tab separates desktop control, the Genesis browser, your browsers, and documents. More apps adds services connected through MCP. Turning one on does not give every other category access. These permissions govern tools; a model request does not automatically override them.
steps.checkpoint: You can identify each category and its state.

steps.title: Allow the access your task needs
steps.narrationDraft: Enable the category needed for the task you intend, and check the per-browser or per-server entries. Computer use changes apply immediately. Browser Bridge and an MCP server must also be connected before their controls work.
steps.checkpoint: Only the intended task’s access is enabled.

steps.title: Use handoff while you act
steps.narrationDraft: When Genesis is controlling your desktop, the control bar can let you Take control. Use it before typing into the same surface. Once you finish, return control with Resume only if you want the automation to continue. Read its status after the handoff.
steps.checkpoint: You know how to avoid competing mouse and keyboard input.

steps.title: Read tools separately from permissions
steps.narrationDraft: In Settings → Plugins → Skills, individual tool switches can restrict available actions. A connected service, enabled tool and permitted computer category may all be needed for the same task. If an action is unavailable, check those layers rather than simply enabling everything.
steps.checkpoint: You know where to check an unavailable action.

sourceLessons.title: Tools, plugins and connected apps
sourceLessons.prerequisites: Settings → Plugins. Only install packages you trust.

steps.title: Skills are the actions Genesis can use
steps.narrationDraft: Open Plugins → Skills. Search for a tool to read its description and switch it on or off. A tool is an action; a skill can give instructions for using tools. Turning off an action can make a task unavailable. AI-created tools have their own controls.
steps.checkpoint: You can locate a tool and understand what it does.

steps.title: A plugin bundles capabilities
steps.narrationDraft: Open the Plugins tab. Use Add → Import a plugin for a local plugin folder. Importing lets you review the package. Read its capabilities and trust the specific reviewed version before turning it on. Plugins can contain code and instructions that run with Genesis’s access.
steps.checkpoint: You understand that importing and enabling are separate steps.

steps.title: Apps are connected services
steps.narrationDraft: The Apps tab holds service connections and their keys. Set up only the service your task needs, add its key where requested and turn on the connection. A key allows an API connection; it is not always the same as an interactive signed-in account. A connector may have only the capabilities its card describes.
steps.checkpoint: The service’s card shows its configured connection state.

steps.title: MCP connects an outside tool server
steps.narrationDraft: MCP servers is for a service that supplies tools through the Model Context Protocol. Its transport may be local stdio, Streamable HTTP or legacy SSE. Use the server’s documented command or URL, enable it and check that it connects. The server’s individual tools can also be restricted.
steps.checkpoint: You know where the server’s connection and tool list are shown.

steps.title: Hooks run at lifecycle events
steps.narrationDraft: Hooks can run reviewed commands at named events, such as before a tool action. They are an advanced option. A command can deny or modify an action according to its supported hook contract. Review the command and trust its version before enabling it. You do not need hooks for ordinary use.
steps.checkpoint: You can distinguish a hook from a chat tool or app connection.

steps.title: Use the quick page or full Settings
steps.narrationDraft: The left-panel Plugins page is a quick place to browse and switch capabilities. Manage opens fuller Settings controls for keys, imports and server editing. An OpenAI-compatible model endpoint does not automatically connect OpenAI account apps or every connector. Check the exact feature the integration offers.
steps.checkpoint: You know when to use the quick page and when to open Manage.

sourceLessons.title: Let Genesis work on code safely
sourceLessons.prerequisites: A code folder you own. Git available or the optional Git setup offered in Settings.

steps.title: Add the folder in Code
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Code → Overview. Add the code folder you want Genesis to work on. The page explains whether Git is ready. Git is the version tool used for snapshots and safe copies; if missing, Genesis can offer an optional private download with your consent.
steps.checkpoint: The intended code folder appears in the list.

steps.title: Use undo history
steps.narrationDraft: Open History. Snapshots record versions around Genesis’s edits. Take a snapshot now gives you a point you can return to. A snapshot is a saved code version, not a backup of all Genesis memories or your entire computer.
steps.checkpoint: You can see snapshots for the chosen code folder.

steps.title: Go back to an earlier version
steps.narrationDraft: Inspect Changes before choosing Go back here. Genesis takes a “Before going back” snapshot so that return is itself undoable. Select the correct folder and snapshot; unrelated files or data are outside the promise of a code snapshot.
steps.checkpoint: You know which saved version you are restoring.

steps.title: Try risky changes in a safe copy
steps.narrationDraft: Open Safe copies, choose the folder and name the experiment. Make a safe copy creates a separate working folder. Ask Genesis to work in that copy. The original stays available while you inspect the experiment’s result.
steps.checkpoint: The copy has a separate path you can give Genesis.

steps.title: Review before bringing changes back
steps.narrationDraft: Open the copy’s Changes or start a Code review. A review looks for likely problems; it is not proof that code works. Test the result. Bring back applies the copy’s changes to the original, with an undo point. Read any clash before choosing which version to keep.
steps.checkpoint: You have inspected and tested the changes before bringing them back.

steps.title: Keep local versions separate from online publication
steps.narrationDraft: Saving a code snapshot is local. Uploading code, creating a GitHub repository or opening a pull request makes an outward change and has separate controls. The next lesson walks through that connection.
steps.checkpoint: You can distinguish a local save from a GitHub upload.

sourceLessons.title: Connect GitHub and share code
sourceLessons.prerequisites: A GitHub account and a token with access appropriate to the repository.

steps.title: Connect in Code → GitHub
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Code → GitHub. Paste your GitHub token in the connection field and connect. A token is an access credential; keep it private and give it the access required for your intended repositories. Confirm the displayed account.
steps.checkpoint: The page shows the intended connected account.

steps.title: Download a repository or select a folder
steps.narrationDraft: The repository list can download a repository to a code folder. A repository is a project stored with version history. If you already have a local folder, add it under Code first. Confirm the download destination before editing.
steps.checkpoint: The intended repository or folder is available locally.

steps.title: Save local work before uploading
steps.narrationDraft: Inspect changed files and use the history/save controls to record a clear local change. A commit is a labelled saved version. A local save does not by itself upload code to GitHub. Include a short message explaining what changed.
steps.checkpoint: You can identify the local change you intend to upload.

steps.title: Choose the outward action deliberately
steps.narrationDraft: Put on GitHub creates an online repository from a folder; choose its name and privacy. Upload sends local committed changes to the configured remote. Open pull request proposes changes for review. These are distinct actions. Inspect the destination and visible result before confirming.
steps.checkpoint: The repository, privacy and proposed change are the ones you intended.

steps.title: Get updates and review the result
steps.narrationDraft: Get updates brings remote changes into a connected local folder. Conflicts may need attention when both copies changed. Open the GitHub result to verify the upload or pull request. Posting a code review to GitHub shares it with people who can see that pull request.
steps.checkpoint: You can find the final repository or pull request and check its contents.

sourceLessons.title: Connect your phone or Telegram
sourceLessons.prerequisites: Genesis running on the computer. Android app for pairing, or a Telegram bot token for Telegram.

steps.title: Your computer is still the engine
steps.narrationDraft: The phone app and Telegram can talk to the desktop Genesis. They do not move the whole AI, models or memory onto the phone. Keep the computer’s Genesis running and reachable. A phone connection and a Telegram connection are separate setup choices.
steps.checkpoint: You understand where the model and work are running.

steps.title: Pair the Android app
steps.narrationDraft: Use Pair Mobile Device in the left panel or the phone step in Finish setting up. Follow the displayed pairing flow in the Android app. Treat the pairing information as private. Confirm the intended device is connected before asking it to control desktop work.
steps.checkpoint: Your intended phone completes pairing.

steps.title: Connect a Telegram bot
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Communications. Get a bot token through Telegram’s BotFather, enter it in Bot token, enable the bridge and save. Open your bot in Telegram and press Start. The page’s status shows whether the bridge has connected.
steps.checkpoint: Your bot replies and the desktop shows it connected.

steps.title: Restrict who may control the bot
steps.narrationDraft: Check Allowed users. After messaging the bot, the Allow only… action can restrict control to your chat. An empty list uses the first chat that messages it, so explicitly restricting the intended chat is clearer for an unattended setup.
steps.checkpoint: Only the intended Telegram user may control Genesis.

steps.title: Choose how much reaches Telegram
steps.narrationDraft: Activity on Telegram offers Silent, Status and Verbose. Status edits one live activity card; Verbose sends more steps. Telegram alert controls can mute sounds or temporarily pause alerts. /unplug disconnects the bridge; you can enable it again from Genesis.
steps.checkpoint: The phone receives the amount of activity you intended.

steps.title: Answer a needs-you request once
steps.narrationDraft: Approvals, codes and challenges can reach the desktop, paired phone and Telegram. The first valid answer wins. Optional email-code reading and phone SMS-code forwarding have separate settings and permissions. Start with manual answers until you understand those options.
steps.checkpoint: You know where to answer a request and which connections receive it.

sourceLessons.title: When Genesis needs your help
sourceLessons.prerequisites: An action or mission that has requested owner input.

steps.title: Read the request before answering
steps.narrationDraft: Discoveries and the connected communication surfaces can show requests for help. Read what action is proposed, its destination and the result it expects. Approve only the actual action you intend. An ambiguous request is a good reason to ask for clarification.
steps.checkpoint: You can state exactly what you are approving.

steps.title: Keep sign-in and verification deliberate
steps.narrationDraft: A site may need a login, verification code or CAPTCHA. Complete the required step through the offered handoff. Genesis does not solve a CAPTCHA for you. A code request should belong to the sign-in you expect, not an unrelated message.
steps.checkpoint: The correct request is answered on the intended site.

steps.title: Decline or explain a different choice
steps.narrationDraft: If the request is wrong, decline it and explain the change you want. If it simply needs more facts, answer those facts. An approval is specific to the request; it is not a blanket promise that all later actions are approved.
steps.checkpoint: Your decision accurately expresses what you want next.

steps.title: Check the final deliverable
steps.narrationDraft: Projects wait in Review and missions have owner sign-off. Open the actual file, page or result before accepting. A model saying “finished” is not the same as your acceptance. If it falls short, describe the missing result in plain words.
steps.checkpoint: You accept work based on its result.

sourceLessons.title: Keep a small companion on your desktop
sourceLessons.prerequisites: The Genesis desktop app on Windows.

steps.title: Open Desktop pet
steps.narrationDraft: Open Settings → Computer use → Desktop pet, or View → Mini & Pets. The page shows the pets available in your version. Choose the one you like and turn on Show pet on desktop, or click Show mini. These desktop preferences apply immediately.
steps.checkpoint: The selected pet appears on your desktop.

steps.title: Use its little controls
steps.narrationDraft: Drag its handle to move it. The small chat, voice and menu controls give quick access to Genesis. The pet is a doorway into the same app, not a separate model or a new memory.
steps.checkpoint: You know how to move it and open Genesis.

steps.title: Show or hide it when convenient
steps.narrationDraft: Use the page’s Show/Hide mini control. The shortcut shown in Settings can focus the pet when available; if another app owns the shortcut, use Show mini instead. The selected desktop pet can return at the next Genesis start.
steps.checkpoint: You can show and hide the companion without losing your conversation.

sourceLessons.title: Give file tools the right working folder
sourceLessons.prerequisites: Settings → System → Tool access. Know the folder your task needs.

steps.title: Find the workspace
steps.narrationDraft: Workspace shows Genesis’s normal working folder. It follows the installation automatically. Ask Genesis to put a result there when you do not need a different location. This is separate from adding a Git folder under Code.
steps.checkpoint: You can locate the folder where ordinary outputs belong.

steps.title: Allow another folder only when needed
steps.narrationDraft: Additional allowed write paths lists other folders the file tools may write to, one path per line. Add the exact project folder your intended task needs, then save. Do not add the whole computer simply to silence an error. Permissions and service connections are separate layers.
steps.checkpoint: The allowed path is the specific folder you intended.

steps.title: Protect important files
steps.narrationDraft: Protected files names files that should be kept protected from tool writes. Core read-only protects Genesis’s core identity from its own modification. These controls apply to supported tool paths; they are not an operating-system sandbox for every third-party program or shell command.
steps.checkpoint: You understand which tool boundary the setting provides.

steps.title: Give commands enough time
steps.narrationDraft: Bash timeout (s) limits how long a shell command may run through that tool. A long build may need more time than a short listing. Change a timeout for a known need, save, and inspect the actual command result. A longer timeout does not repair a wrong command.
steps.checkpoint: You can distinguish a timed-out command from a model connection problem.

audio.rationale: Decoded length 106.4135 s. Opening begins with music (-16.7 dB RMS in first half-second); from 0.5 s it is established near -13 dB. Ending remains musical through 105.5 s, then drops to -39.3 dB RMS at 106 s. Repeat 0.5–105.5 s, keeping the opening once, with equal-power 4 s overlaps over the late recovery (101.5–105.5 s). Retain the musical breakdown at 98.5–103 s; it is low-level music, not silence. Use 3 s opening / 7 s closing fades only at the video ends.

scenes.body: A site may need a login, verification code or CAPTCHA. Complete the required step through the offered handoff. Genesis does not solve a CAPTCHA for you.
scenes.note: Step 2 of 4 · Teaching 1 of 2. Locate the highlighted control.

scenes.title:
The sign-in
you expected
scenes.body: A code request should belong to the sign-in you expect, not an unrelated message.
scenes.note: Step 2 of 4 · Teaching 2 of 2. Read this distinction before acting.

scenes.title:
An expected
verification step
items: Check the intended site and account
Use the offered owner handoff
Complete the required site check yourself
Return control after checking the result
scenes.note: Genesis does not solve a CAPTCHA for you. An unexpected code can belong to a different sign-in.

scenes.title:
Pause and
check this
items: The correct request is answered on the intended site.
scenes.note: Try it in Genesis. Pause for as long as you need. Continue when you can explain or confirm this result.

scenes.title:
Decline or
explain a change
scenes.body: If the request is wrong, decline it and explain the change you want. If it simply needs more facts, answer those facts.
scenes.note: Step 3 of 4 · Teaching 1 of 2. Locate the highlighted control.

scenes.title:
Decline or
explain a change
scenes.body: An approval is specific to the request; it is not a blanket promise that all later actions are approved.
scenes.note: Step 3 of 4 · Teaching 2 of 2. Read this distinction before acting.

scenes.title:
Say what
you mean
items: Decline an action you do not want
Explain the changed destination or result
Answer missing facts when that is the need
Read the specific updated request
scenes.note: Example: “Draft this message, but do not send it.” One approval does not approve every later action.

scenes.title:
Pause and
check this
items: Your decision accurately expresses what you want next.
scenes.note: Try it in Genesis. Pause for as long as you need. Continue when you can explain or confirm this result.

scenes.title:
Inspect the
final result
scenes.body: Projects wait in Review and missions have owner sign-off. Open the actual file, page or result before accepting. A model saying “finished” is not the same as your acceptance.
scenes.note: Step 4 of 4 · Teaching 1 of 2. Locate the highlighted control.

scenes.title:
Inspect the
final result
scenes.body: If it falls short, describe the missing result in plain words.
scenes.note: Step 4 of 4 · Teaching 2 of 2. Read this distinction before acting.

scenes.title:
Accept the
actual work
items: Open the project’s file from Review
Compare it with your requested result
For a mission, read owner sign-off conditions
Describe any missing part before accepting
scenes.note: A model’s finished message and your acceptance are separate. Inspect the real delivery and its source material.

scenes.title:
Pause and
check this
items: You accept work based on its result.
scenes.note: Try it in Genesis. Pause for as long as you need. Continue when you can explain or confirm this result.

you begin
items: The Genesis desktop app on Windows.

desktop companion

scenes.note: Step 1 of 3 · Teaching 1 of 2. Locate the highlighted control.

Choose your
desktop companion
scenes.body: Choose the one you like and turn on Show pet on desktop, or click Show mini. These desktop preferences apply immediately.
scenes.callout: Show mini · Show pet on desktop
scenes.note: Step 1 of 3 · Teaching 2 of 2. Read this distinction before acting.

items: Genesis AI Earth
Terminator - Calm / Terminator 1 - Active
Conversation Orb - Calm
Conversation Orb - Active
scenes.note: These are the five pets in this version of Genesis. Choose the one you like; the available collection can vary by version.

collection
scenes.body: The current Settings list and mini menu offer five pets. Choose a style you like; all of them open the same Genesis app.
scenes.note: The two Terminator styles and two Conversation Orb styles are separate choices, alongside Genesis AI Earth.

scenes.note: Try it in Genesis. Pause for as long as you need. Continue when you can explain or confirm this result.

Quick access
to the same app
scenes.body: Drag its handle to move it. The small chat, voice and menu controls give quick access to Genesis. The pet is a doorway into the same app, not a separate model or a new memory.
scenes.note: Step 2 of 3. Locate the highlighted control.

scenes.title:
The same
Genesis doorway
items: Drag the top handle to move the mini
Chat opens your Genesis conversation
Voice opens its voice controls
Menu offers pets, Settings and Hide mini
scenes.note: The mini uses the same app, model and memory. It is a convenient doorway, not a new conversation engine.

scenes.note: Try it in Genesis. Pause for as long as you need. Continue when you can explain or confirm this result.

and focus
scenes.body: Use the page’s Show/Hide mini control. The shortcut shown in Settings can focus the pet when available; if another app owns the shortcut, use Show mini instead.

and focus

Show pet on desktop controls the preference
Alt + Win + P can show and focus it
If the shortcut is busy, use Show mini

scenes.title:
The right folder.
The right boundary.
scenes.body:
Give file tools the right working folder
Workspace, allowed writes, protection and timeouts.

scenes.title:
Before
you begin
items: Settings → System → Tool access. Know the folder your task needs.
scenes.note: Prepare these prerequisites before trying the lesson. Pause whenever you need time in Genesis.

scenes.title:
Find the
working folder
scenes.body: Workspace shows Genesis’s normal working folder. It follows the installation automatically. Ask Genesis to put a result there when you do not need a different location.
scenes.note: Step 1 of 4 · Teaching 1 of 2. Locate the highlighted control.

scenes.title:
Find the
working folder
scenes.body: This is separate from adding a Git folder under Code.
scenes.note: Step 1 of 4 · Teaching 2 of 2. Read this distinction before acting.

scenes.title:
Ordinary output
or code folder?
items: Read Workspace under System → Tool access
Use that folder for ordinary outputs
Code selects a versioned project folder
Specify the path when a different folder is needed
scenes.note: The normal workspace follows the installation. Adding a Git folder under Code is a separate operation.

scenes.title:
Pause and
check this
items: You can locate the folder where ordinary outputs belong.
scenes.note: Try it in Genesis. Pause for as long as you need. Continue when you can explain or confirm this result.

scenes.title:
Allow a
specific folder
scenes.body: Additional allowed write paths lists other folders the file tools may write to, one path per line. Add the exact project folder your intended task needs, then save.
scenes.note: Step 2 of 4 · Teaching 1 of 2. Locate the highlighted control.

scenes.title:
Allow a
specific folder
scenes.body: Do not add the whole computer simply to silence an error. Permissions and service connections are separate layers.
scenes.note: Step 2 of 4 · Teaching 2 of 2. Read this distinction before acting.

scenes.title:
A specific
write destination
items: Add the exact project folder path
Use one allowed folder per line
Save the intended path list
Check the resulting file location
scenes.note: Example: allow a disposable practice folder. Do not add every drive simply to bypass a failed write.

scenes.title:
Pause and
check this
items: The allowed path is the specific folder you intended.
scenes.note: Try it in Genesis. Pause for as long as you need. Continue when you can explain or confirm this result.

scenes.title:
Understand the
protection boundary
scenes.body: Protected files names files that should be kept protected from tool writes. Core read-only protects Genesis’s core identity from its own modification.
scenes.note: Step 3 of 4 · Teaching 1 of 2. Locate the highlighted control.

scenes.title:
Understand the
protection boundary
scenes.body: These controls apply to supported tool paths; they are not an operating-system sandbox for every third-party program or shell command.
scenes.note: Step 3 of 4 · Teaching 2 of 2. Read this distinction before acting.

scenes.title:
A supported
tool boundary
items: Protected files restrict supported tool writes
Core read-only protects core identity paths
Read which path the setting covers
A shell or outside program has its own effects
scenes.note: These controls are not an operating-system sandbox for every command. Keep important data protected through the appropriate boundary.

scenes.title:
Pause and
check this
items: You understand which tool boundary the setting provides.
scenes.note: Try it in Genesis. Pause for as long as you need. Continue when you can explain or confirm this result.

scenes.title:
Time for a
known command
scenes.body: Bash timeout (s) limits how long a shell command may run through that tool. A long build may need more time than a short listing.
scenes.note: Step 4 of 4 · Teaching 1 of 2. Locate the highlighted control.

scenes.title:
Time for a
known command
scenes.body: Change a timeout for a known need, save, and inspect the actual command result. A longer timeout does not repair a wrong command.
scenes.note: Step 4 of 4 · Teaching 2 of 2. Read this distinction before acting.

scenes.title:
A known
longer build
items: Read the actual command and result
Increase Bash timeout for a known slow job
Save the change and inspect the next run
Separate timeout from provider failure
scenes.note: More time cannot repair a wrong command, a missing file or a disconnected model. Diagnose the actual error.

scenes.title:
Pause and
check this
items: You can distinguish a timed-out command from a model connection problem.
scenes.note: Try it in Genesis. Pause for as long as you need. Continue when you can explain or confirm this result.
